Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 SUMMARY 2 OVERVIEW OF PLAY 3 START CARD 4 FINISH CARDS 5 GAME END 6 Guidance for Communication 7 VARIANTS SUMMARY Attempt to find your paradise island on the good ship Tranquility! All you need to do is fill a 6x6 sea grid with Island cards (which are numbered 1-80) and have played one Start and one Finish card. • You all win once the grid is complete and the Start and Finish cards have been placed, living out your days on an island paradise. • You all lose if a single player can no longer play or discard any cards, causing the ship to be lost at sea forever. OVERVIEW OF PLAY You may NOT communicate with other players except when discussing the Start card. Everyone starts with 5 cards in their hand and a their own draw pile. On your turn you must take one of the following actions: A) Play 1 card from your hand, or B) Discard two cards from your hand. After taking an action you must draw back up to a hand of five cards. The cards come from the top of your own draw pile. If your draw pile runs out, continue playing until the game ends. A) Play a Card Select an Island card from your hand and play it anywhere in the grid, providing you follow these rules: 1. Cards must be placed on the grid so that their numbers ascends from lowest to highest, starting at the bottom-left corner and ending in the top-right. On each row, cards to the right must be a higher number than cards on their left. All the cards on a row must be higher numbers than the cards on the rows below. 2. If the card is placed next to an existing card in the sequence (even if they are on different rows), then you must discard a number of cards from your hand equal to the difference between the two card numbers EXAMPLE: placing a ‘5’ next to a ‘3’ means you must discard two cards because 5-3=2. If a card is played between two cards, discard cards the least number of cards to make up the difference between your card and one to either side of it. EXAMPLE: You play a 6 between 3 and 7. Discard 1 card because 7-6=1 and 6-3=3. Always discard the least. You may not place a card if that would require you to discard more than the four cards remaining in your hand. You may not discard cards from your draw pile. B) Discard two cards You may discard two cards rather if you cannot legally play a card or because you choose to. START CARD Every player has one Start Card in their draw deck. When you draw a Start card and nobody has played one yet, you must play that Start card as your action this turn. The Start card is not placed within the grid but in the bottom left-hand corner of the frame. Then a total of eight cards, divided among players, must be discarded from hand. You may discuss HOW MANY CARDS each of you is willing to discard but not specifics about what is in your hand or where you might wish to play cards in the future. After discarding, all players draw back up to a hand of five cards. If the Start space has already been filled, the remaining Start cards have no purpose and may be discarded per normal rules. FINISH CARDS There are 5 Finish Cards in the game. You may only play a Finish card once you have finished completely filling in the grid with cards (plus a Start card). You cannot win without a Finish card being played. Prior to completing the grid, Finish Cards may be discarded like any other card during your turn. GAME END You all win if the active player successfully plays a Finish card after the grid is complete. You all lose if any player cannot take a legal action on their turn. This could be because they can’t play a card into the grid, either because it doesn’t fit numerically, or because the player doesn’t have enough cards to discard in order to play it, o --- Jump on board the good ship Tranquility and set sail for paradise. Take care, though, because in a land where the day blends into night it's easy to lose track of time and you still need to find that special little island to call home. Tranquility is a co-operative card game in which players must fill the sea with islands — specifically island cards with numbers on them — and guide the ship home before any player runs out of cards. Note that in the world of Tranquility, the only way to play is in silence. --- The goal of the game is for the team to complete the grid before any player runs out of available actions. Cards must be placed so that the grid ascends in numerical order from bottom left to top right. All the players win if they manage to complete the grid and have placed a Start and Finish card. All players lose if a single player can no longer play or discard any cards legally following the instructions given below. The players may not, however, communicate. Play is taken in turns moving clockwise with the quietest player going first. On a player’s turn they must do one of the following: 1. Play a card or 2. Discard two cards. Then they must draw back up to a hand of five cards. Cards must be placed so that the grid ascends in numerical order from bottom left to top right. If the card is placed next to an existing card in the sequence then they must discard cards from their hand equal to the difference between the numbers face down in front of them e.g. placing a 5 next to a 3 will require two cards to be discarded from their hand. This applies even if the cards are on different rows. —description from the publisher
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Backed on KS in 2019 - STILL waiting for it to arrive (Feb 2021). AND STILL WAITING (JUN 2021) and the company isn't returning my email. Will re-rate when I get a chance to play - giving a 1 to hopefully draw attention to my unfulfilled order.

[Rating: 1/10] The company better hire a better person to handle the PR. Defensive and sarcastic towards backers and always felt he knows everything. There are better games out there besides this.

[Rating: 3/10] Takes too much space to play and it is difficult to keep cards lined up properly (half of the game is fixing cards position). Bought it second hand and I think I will resell it pretty soon.

[Rating: 3/10] After 1 play on BGA: There’s a whole bunch of games where you have to sort numbered cards while respecting their order. At first, things go fairly well, but toward the end, it gradually falls apart. So I spend most of the game just hoping it will hold together for as long as possible… until the inevitable happens and I don’t gain the points I was aiming for. Avoiding damage under constant tension — all in all, that’s not a game experience I find particularly enjoyable.

[Rating: 3/10] Unimpressive rulebook and number climbing.  In the bottom three from 2020, beaten only by covid and a questionable tattoo decision.

[Rating: 4/10] cooperative hand management game. Definitely a cerebral activity, where I'm not that invested in the outcome.

[Rating: 4/10] I tried it solo and multiplayer. What you must do and how you must "play" the mechanics of the game seems clear enough. Maybe the expansion modules included in the box blur things a little bit, but as such, I didn't feel much inclined to play it again.

[Rating: 4/10] Only tried solo on BGA. Solo - it's a pretty simple memory puzzle  I don't really see the point - you know every number is going to come out.  As a co-op, I can see it could be fun a couple times, but I think it would be frustrating for those with perfect memory. I'd prefer something that doesn't feel as much of a math puzzle and has more control (i.e. having all the cards in your hand and deciding how to play them).  I do enjoy some limited communication co-ops like The Crew and The Grizzled, but a silent co-op.... nah.

[Rating: 4/10] I didn't really like this game.  It was a co-op game but it feels more like a solitaire game with other players screwing up your plays.

[Rating: 4/10] Pretty fun. Zen experience. Just a tad too much card counting for it to be really something I'd play in the background while having a nice chat with someone or so.

[Rating: 4/10] Strong sense of a pedestrian old-school solitaire game, the final jigsaw piece of victory feeling mostly down to the luck of the deck. Entirely forgettable theme.

[Rating: 4/10] You can lose early but you have no way of knowing until the end of the game.  It's interesting to think about how co-op games resolve early losses; the short length of these games help sort of make this implementation mysterious.
